projects.name: packtpublishing/c-plus-plus-memory-management (book techniques)
projects.lead: Listed as: Code a C++ book benchmarks or cites; see techniques (claim words: None; licence tag: MIT; book: C++ Memory Management (2025), ch. 10 Arena-Based Memory Management and Other Optimizations, sections 'Looking at the numbers' and 'Generalizing to SizeBasedArena<T,N>') Book techniques, one candidate record each if the repo carries the code: SizeBasedArena<T,N> (Orc Tribe size-based bump arena): Homemade operator new took 76.4% of standard-library time and operator delete 8.03% (Meyers singleton); global singleton made delete a no-op. [measured: Allocate then destroy 1,000,000 16-byte Orc objects, single thread, std::chrono timing in microseconds, one run, online gcc 15 at -O2, CPU not stated. Baseline is the standard library operator new/delete. new: 23433 us standard, 17906 us Meyers-singleton arena, 17573 us global-singleton arena. delete: 7943 us standard, 638 us Meyers, 0 us global. Reuse of freed memory is not supported, so not like for like.] (book: C++ Memory Management (2025), ch. 10 Arena-Based Memory Management and Other Optimizations, sections 'Looking at the numbers' and 'Generalizing to SizeBasedArena<T,N>'); ChunkSizedAllocator<N,Sz...> (chunked fixed-size-class pool): Chunked version ran in 12,032 versus 13,360 for the standard version, about 90.05% of the standard library time. [measured: 300,000 allocations (100,000 each of 30-, 60- and 100-byte objects) then destroy and deallocate through std::function, microseconds, one run, online gcc 15 at -O2, CPU not stated. Baseline is standard operator new/delete. The upfront pool allocation in the constructor is not timed. The book warns locking the mutex strongly affects the gain and deallocate locking would likely erase it.] (book: C++ Memory Management (2025), ch. 10 Arena-Based Memory Management and Other Optimizations, sections 'Chunked pools' and 'Testing ChunkSizedAllocator'); Sequential buffer allocator (seq_buf_allocator) with std::vector and Vector<T,A>: Book says the test shows interesting performance with the sequential buffer allocator, and the book's Vector<T,A> outperforms std::vector<T,A>; no numbers printed. [measured: 500,000 push_back insertions of a one-int struct after reserve, timed in microseconds with std::chrono, default allocator against the sequential buffer allocator, for std::vector and the book's Vector. Compiler, flags and CPU not stated, results not printed.] (book: C++ Memory Management (2025), ch. 14, Example usage - a sequential buffer allocator (companion code in chapter14)); Vector<T> with allocation separated from construction: Naive version default-constructs elements that are then overwritten; the rewrite aims to get closer to std::vector performance by doing minimal work. (book: C++ Memory Management (2025), ch. 12 end, A more efficient Vector<T> and Using low-level standard facilities)
